topic: Fever Management and Tepid Sponging
subtopic: SAQ 1.1
stem: Distinguish between fever and hyperthermia, and define the four physical methods of body heat loss.
options: In fever, the hypothalamus raises the thermoregulatory set-point to maintain a controlled elevation of core temperature; in hyperthermia, core temperature rises beyond hypothalamic set-point control. Four heat-loss methods: Conduction (direct contact with a cooler object), Convection (warmed air rising and replaced by cooler air), Radiation (warming nearby objects without contact), and Evaporation (liquid sweat turning into vapour on the skin).

Onset (chill phase): shivering, cold pale skin, gooseflesh, increased HR/RR, no sweating. Course (plateau): warm skin, no chills, tachycardia/tachypnoea, dehydration, malaise, drowsiness. Abatement (flush): warm flushed skin, sweating, less shivering. Reduction stages: Lysis (gradual drop over 3–5 days with improved pulse/RR), Crisis (sharp drop within 24 hrs with improved pulse/RR), False/Pseudocrisis (drop without pulse/RR or clinical improvement, soon rising again).

Explain procedure/screen bed -> replace clothing with 2 bath blankets -> pour 26–32°C solution -> place wrung flannels on forehead, axillae, groins, back of neck, and abdomen (change every 5 min) -> expose one limb at a time, sponge with long strokes leaving beads to evaporate with air movement -> check temp at 10–15 min -> discontinue once temperature drops by 1–2°C -> offer high-calorie diet and 2.5–3 L fluids -> recheck/chart at 30 min -> dry, dress, tidy, and document.

Assessments: check purpose of cool application, baseline vital signs, fluid/electrolyte status, skin condition before/after, and prior antipyretics/antibiotics. Top shelf: basin, solution (water ± alcohol), 8 washcloths/flannels, bath thermometer (26–32°C), patient thermometer, powder/hairbrush, cold drink if permitted. Bottom shelf: 2 bath blankets, clean bed sheets, bucket for used water, jug of water.

Four heat-loss methods: Conduction (direct contact with a cooler object), Convection (warmed air rising and replaced by cooler air), Radiation (warming nearby objects without contact), and Evaporation (liquid sweat turning into vapour on the skin).

topic: Maintaining Skin Integrity and Pressure Ulcer Prevention
subtopic: SAQ 2.1
stem: Define pressure sore, list eight risk factors for impaired skin integrity, and identify eight common vulnerable pressure areas.
options: 1. Assess risk using the Braden Scale; 2. Reposition every 2 hours; 3. Use proper lifting techniques avoiding shear; 4. Keep skin clean, dry, and free of urine/faeces/drainage; 5. Apply zinc oxide cream to sacrum/elbows/heels and cornstarch powder; 6. Keep linens dry and wrinkle-free; 7. Avoid skin trauma (e.g., chipped bedpans); 8. Provide pressure-relieving mattresses/support devices; 9. Ensure protein-rich nutrition, fluids, and active/ROM exercises.

A pressure sore (decubitus ulcer) is a localized injury to skin and underlying tissue over a bony prominence or medical device caused by prolonged pressure, friction, or shear impairing blood flow. Eight risk factors: immobility, excessive heat, inadequate nutrition, advanced age, friction/shear, chronic illness, faecal/urinary incontinence, decreased mental status (others: poor lifting, diminished sensation, hard surfaces, tight bandages/splints). Eight pressure areas: coccyx/sacrum, greater trochanter/ischium, heels, elbows, scapulae, patellae, malleoli, and occiput (plus ears, obese skin folds, under breasts).

Stage I: intact skin with non-blanchable erythema. Stage II: partial-thickness loss of epidermis/dermis (blister/shallow crater). Stage III: full-thickness loss into subcutaneous tissue down to fascia. Stage IV: full-thickness loss with extensive necrosis/damage to muscle, bone, or tendons. Exudates: Serous (clear fluid), Sanguinous (bloody), Serosanguinous (blood mixed with clear fluid), Purulent (cloudy, viscous, pus-like).

Explain procedure, ensure privacy, wash hands, inspect skin/mucosa colour against racial baseline, feel temperature with back of hand/fingers (reflects dermal blood circulation), inspect moisture/dryness/odours, gently pinch skin for turgor/return speed (reflects hydration), press ankle for pitting oedema, test sensation, and check for lesions or ecchymosis/petechiae/purpura.

stem: Summarize nine key nursing strategies for preventing pressure ulcers in bedridden clients.
options: Stage I: intact skin with non-blanchable erythema. Stage II: partial-thickness loss of epidermis/dermis (blister/shallow crater). Stage III: full-thickness loss into subcutaneous tissue down to fascia. Stage IV: full-thickness loss with extensive necrosis/damage to muscle, bone, or tendons. Exudates: Serous (clear fluid), Sanguinous (bloody), Serosanguinous (blood mixed with clear fluid), Purulent (cloudy, viscous, pus-like).

1. Assess risk using the Braden Scale; 2. Reposition every 2 hours; 3. Use proper lifting techniques avoiding shear; 4. Keep skin clean, dry, and free of urine/faeces/drainage; 5. Apply zinc oxide cream to sacrum/elbows/heels and cornstarch powder; 6. Keep linens dry and wrinkle-free; 7. Avoid skin trauma (e.g., chipped bedpans); 8. Provide pressure-relieving mattresses/support devices; 9. Ensure protein-rich nutrition, fluids, and active/ROM exercises.

Explain procedure, ensure privacy, wash hands, inspect skin/mucosa colour against racial baseline, feel temperature with back of hand/fingers (reflects dermal blood circulation), inspect moisture/dryness/odours, gently pinch skin for turgor/return speed (reflects hydration), press ankle for pitting oedema, test sensation, and check for lesions or ecchymosis/petechiae/purpura.

A pressure sore (decubitus ulcer) is a localized injury to skin and underlying tissue over a bony prominence or medical device caused by prolonged pressure, friction, or shear impairing blood flow. Eight risk factors: immobility, excessive heat, inadequate nutrition, advanced age, friction/shear, chronic illness, faecal/urinary incontinence, decreased mental status (others: poor lifting, diminished sensation, hard surfaces, tight bandages/splints). Eight pressure areas: coccyx/sacrum, greater trochanter/ischium, heels, elbows, scapulae, patellae, malleoli, and occiput (plus ears, obese skin folds, under breasts).

topic: Therapeutic Positioning in Nursing
subtopic: SAQ 3.1
stem: Define positioning in nursing, state its four rationales, and list six general principles nurses must follow when positioning a patient.
options: Prone: back burns/sores/surgeries, >24 hrs post-lower-limb amputation, renal biopsy, improving oxygenation in ARDS. Lateral: periodic turning of bedridden clients and immediate post-op aspiration prevention (excluding spinal/epidural anaesthesia). Sims's: vaginal/rectal exam, enema/suppository, sigmoidoscopy/proctoscopy. Lithotomy: vaginal delivery/exam, vaginal hysterectomy, haemorrhoidectomy/fissurotomy.

Trendelenburg: place patient supine and tilt the entire bed frame head-down using a bed key or bed blocks at the foot end (Indications: postural drainage, hypotension/shock, DVT). Genupectoral: instruct client to kneel supporting weight on knees and chest with arms extended past head and head turned on a pillow (Indications: rectal exam, enema/suppository administration, obstetric cord prolapse).

Positioning is placing a patient in good body alignment as needed therapeutically. Four rationales: promote comfort, prevent immobility complications, stimulate circulation, promote normal physiological functions. Six general principles: maintain good body mechanics, obtain assistance as needed, ensure firm mattress at working height, keep sheets clean/dry, avoid resting one body part over another, plan a 24-hour turning schedule (plus ensure comfort and wash hands before/after).

Purposes: relieve/minimize dyspnoea and relieve tension on abdominal sutures. Rationales: thigh roll prevents knee hyperextension and popliteal artery occlusion; arm pillows prevent shoulder dislocation and arm/wrist flexion contractures; ankle pillow prevents heel pressure; footboard maintains dorsiflexion and prevents foot drop.

topic: Collection of Urine Specimens
subtopic: SAQ 4.1
stem: Define random, clean-catch midstream, catheterized, and 24-hour timed urine specimens and state the primary clinical use of each.
options: Explain procedure and post a bathroom sign with date/time -> obtain labelled lab bottle with preservative (HCl or thymol) and keep refrigerated or on ice -> have client void and discard initial specimen at start time -> pour all subsequent voids over 24 hrs into bottle -> have client void at exact end time and add to bottle -> transport promptly to lab -> document start/end times, urine colour/appearance, and voiding pain.

Responsibilities: (1) protect comfort/privacy/cultural beliefs, (2) explain purpose and steps, (3) maintain strict asepsis, (4) record relevant clinical/medication info on requisition slips, (5) transport promptly, and (6) report abnormal results urgently. Transport/storage: send within 2–3 hrs in leak-proof biohazard bags; bacterial culture at room temp; 24-hr specimens refrigerated/on ice; delayed routine samples refrigerated at 4–8°C (long-term frozen ≤-70°C).

Pigments: urochrome, urobilin, uroerythrin (pale yellow to dark amber); specific gravity 1.001–1.025; pH 4.5–8 (avg ~6); volume 1,000–2,500 mL/24 hrs. For infants, cleanse the perineum and urethral opening, attach an adhesive pediatric urine specimen bag to the skin, and gently remove it once adequate urine is collected (or suprapubic aspiration/straight catheter if sterile sample is required).

Random: clean voided sample at any time for routine urinalysis. Clean-catch midstream: sterile mid-void sample after meatal cleansing and flushing initial stream for urine culture. Catheterized: sterile urine aspirated from catheter port or straight catheter for accurate culture. 24-hour timed: full 24-hour collection to evaluate kidney concentrating/diluting function, diabetes/glucose metabolism, creatinine, hormones, or albumin.

topic: Urinary Catheterization: Principles, Female and Male Procedures, and Safety
subtopic: SAQ 5.1
stem: Explain why a patient undergoing non-urological abdominopelvic surgery may require urinary catheterization, and list five contraindications to urethral catheterization.
options: Surgical catheterization keeps the bladder empty to give the surgeon a clearer view and safer palpation of internal tissues, prevents accidental bladder injury, and prevents urine from contaminating perineal sutures. Five contraindications: blood at the meatus (urethral trauma), gross haematuria, urethral infection, urethral pain/discomfort, and patient refusal (also low bladder compliance).

Parts: catheter tip, drainage eye, balloon seal, catheter shaft, drainage funnel, and inflation funnel/balloon port. Types: Intermittent (temporary 5–10 min drainage), Indwelling/Foley (held in place days/weeks by water-filled balloon), Suprapubic (surgically placed through lower abdomen for continuous drainage), External condom (non-invasive sheath adhering externally for incontinence).

Female: urethra 3.7–6.2 cm; cleanse labia/meatus anterior-to-posterior (meatus last) with fresh swabs; insert 5–7.5 cm (+1 inch for balloon); secure to upper thigh with slack. Male: urethra 18–20 cm; retract foreskin, cleanse circularly from meatus to base; hold penis at 90° upward, lubricate 15–18 cm, insert 15–20 cm (to Y-hub) +1 inch; reduce foreskin; secure to thigh or lower abdomen directed toward chest with slack.

Six complications: UTI (urethritis, cystitis, pyelonephritis, bacteraemia—most common), paraphimosis, urethral strictures, urethral perforation, bleeding, and altered micturition. Sediment obstruction is often relieved by catheter flushing, while painful bladder spasms causing extrinsic leakage can be alleviated with anticholinergics such as oxybutynin.

stem: State the five purposes of wound dressing and explain what elevated temperature/pulse and copious fresh blood on a dressing signify during pre-dressing assessment.

stem: Complete this statement about Step-by-Step Sterile Non-Touch Wound Dressing Technique: Wound dressing is a strict sterile non-touch procedure: (1) wash hands, open sterile bowls/receivers aseptically, pour cleansing lotion into gallipot, don facemask and clean gloves; (2) remove adhesive tape slowly while supporting skin and pulling TOWARD the wound (prevents traction/pain along the incision line); (3) lift soiled dressings using dissecting forceps (moistening with sterile normal saline if adhered) and dispose into the destructor bowl; (4) inspect drainage colour/consistency/odour/amount and check for healing or dehiscence, then discard soiled forceps; (5) don sterile gloves and use a paired forceps technique—hold the DISSECTING FORCEPS in the NON-DOMINANT hand to pick up sterile swabs and pass them to the DRESSING FORCEPS in the DOMINANT hand for cleansing, keeping forceps tips pointed downward at all times so fluid does not run back and contaminate the sterile tips; (6) cleanse moving from least to most contaminated—for linear incisions, stroke firmly proximal-to-distal directly over the incision first, then adjacent skin (discarding each swab after one stroke); for irregular wounds, stroke firmly from the centre outward in circular motions using a fresh swab for each circle; dry ____; (7) apply prescribed topical medication and sufficient sterile absorbent gauze—avoiding tight packing in non-bleeding wounds because tight packing forces wound edges apart and delays healing; (8) discard gloves, secure dressing with tape/bandages, reposition client comfortably, wash instruments with clean gloves and pack for CSSD sterilization, clear trolley, wash hands, and document pre/post-dressing wound status (exudate, erythema, granulation) and lotions used.
